lessons.title: Linguistic diversity and dialects
lessons.anelcac: Notions of linguistic diversity, dialects, names of languages, geographical classification
objectives: Becoming aware of the linguistic diversity of Cameroon (about 280 languages according to the LACAGEO Mini-Atlas)
Distinguish language, dialect and variant according to academic definitions
Naming Gbáyá and locating it in the geographical classification of the languages of Cameroon
Adopt an attitude of respect towards all languages

teacher.intro: Lesson: Linguistic diversity and dialects. Module: Module I — Cameroonian linguistic diversity.
steps: **Setting the context:** Display the map of the Linguistic Mini-Atlas of Cameroon. Ask students which languages are spoken in their family.
**Exploration:** Have students read the definitions in the Mini-Atlas (language, dialect, patois, national language). Locate Gbáyá in its linguistic region.
**Conceptualisation:** Explain the language / dialect distinction with examples: the Bulu, Ewondo, Eton and Mangisa dialects all belong to the Beti-Fang language (Mini-Atlas).
**Application:** Complete a table: name of the language, family, main region, ISO code.
**Assessment:** Each student gives an oral presentation of Gbáyá, indicating family and region.
teacher.freedom: The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas (2013) distinguishes about 280 living languages in Cameroon. The exact number varies according to the criteria (SIL: 274, Ethnologue: 279). Value all the languages cited.
teacher.tips: The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas (2013) distinguishes about 280 living languages in Cameroon. The exact number varies according to the criteria (SIL: 274, Ethnologue: 279). Value all the languages cited.

student.intro: Cameroon is one of the richest nations in the world in languages — the linguistic Mini-Atlas lists about 280! In this lesson, you discover the place of Gbáyá in this great family.
activities: Look at the Mini-Atlas map and find the area where Gbáyá is mainly spoken.
Copy and complete: Gbáyá belongs to the ___ family. It is mostly spoken in the ___ region.
According to the Mini-Atlas, how many living languages are there in the Gbáyá region? Note down this number.
Survey: ask an adult the name of the language in which they were raised and where it is spoken.
Memorise: **dialect** = an intelligible variant of the same language; **national language** = language of an ethnic group that does not extend beyond the borders of one State (ACA LAN).
student.memo: Cameroon has about **280 languages** according to the LACAGEO Mini-Atlas. Gbáyá belongs to a Cameroonian language family and has its own dialectal variants. According to the ACA LAN, a national language is the language of an ethnic group that does not extend beyond the borders of one State.

lessons.title: Classification of languages and linguistic atlas
lessons.anelcac: Classification of the languages of Cameroon: linguistic areas, families, ALCAM atlas
objectives: Name the main linguistic areas of Cameroon
Read and interpret an extract from a linguistic atlas (ALCAM / Mini-Atlas)
Classify Gbáyá according to its typological criteria
Producing a short text presenting Gbáyá

teacher.intro: Lesson: Classification of languages and linguistic atlas. Module: Module I — Cameroonian linguistic diversity.
steps: **Setting the context:** Go back over the definitions. How many language families do students remember?
**Presentation:** The 8 world language families according to Ethnologue (Niger-Kordofanian, Nilo-Saharan, Afro-Asiatic…). Place Cameroonian languages within this whole.
**Explanation:** Show how to find Gbáyá in the ALCAM: ISO code, family, location.
**Guided practice:** In pairs, students find 3 languages neighbouring Gbáyá and note their ISO codes.
**Production:** 5-line paragraph presenting Gbáyá (family, region, speakers, distinctive feature).
teacher.freedom: The online ALCAM is on the Mozilla Data Collective. The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas covers all the administrative regions with maps and statistics.
teacher.tips: The online ALCAM is on the Mozilla Data Collective. The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas covers all the administrative regions with maps and statistics.

student.intro: A linguistic atlas is a specialised map. The ALCAM (Atlas of the Languages of Cameroon) and the LACAGEO Mini-Atlas let you locate Gbáyá precisely.
activities: On the Mini-Atlas map, locate Gbáyá and note its administrative region.
List 3 languages whose area is adjacent to that of Gbáyá.
Classify these 4 languages in a table: Language | Family | Main region.
Write an introductory paragraph about Gbáyá with at least 5 pieces of information taken from the atlas.
Memorise: **ISO 639** = international language codes; **ALCAM** = Atlas des Langues du Cameroun.
student.memo: The **ALCAM** and the **LACAGEO Mini-Atlas** list and locate all the national languages of Cameroon. Cameroon has 8 main language families. Gbáyá appears there with its family and its location. Knowing how to read a linguistic atlas is reading the history of peoples.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants
lessons.title: Vowels of Gbáyá
lessons.anelcac: AGLC vowels — simple, specific, complex
objectives: Identify the simple vowels of the phonological system of Gbáyá
Recognising specific vowels absent from French
Pronouncing vowels correctly in the context of a word
Transcribing words containing vowels according to AGLC

vocabulary.frenchText: their mothers have been dead for four years
there are five huts in your village
b) he is lying down but he is not sleeping

teacher.intro: Lesson: Gbáyá vowels. Module: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write known words in Gbáyá on the board and ask which sounds students hear.
**Presentation:** Introduce the AGLC. Write the simple vowels of Gbáyá on the board, articulating them clearly.
**Explanation:** Vowels specific to Gbáyá that are absent from French (nasal, particular openness…). Listening and repetition exercises.
**Application:** List of 10 words — students underline the vowels and indicate: simple or specific.
**Assessment:** Dictation of 5 simple words — students transcribe them with the correct vowels.
teacher.freedom: Use the examples from the platform's ALCAM vocabulary. For each specific vowel, give a memorable key word.
teacher.tips: Use the examples from the platform's ALCAM vocabulary. For each specific vowel, give a memorable key word.

student.intro: Every language has its own sounds. In Gbáyá, some vowels do not exist in French. This lesson teaches you to hear, pronounce and write them.
activities: Listen to the recordings of the Gbáyá vocabulary and identify the vowels you hear.
Classify the vowels: **Shared with French** | **Specific to Gbáyá**.
Transcribe the 5 dictated words, taking care to note each vowel correctly.
Find 3 words in Gbáyá for each specific vowel and write them down.
Memorise: **AGLC** = Alphabet Général des Langues Camerounaises, the official reference.
student.memo: The vowel system of **Gbáyá** includes simple vowels and specific vowels (e.g. nasalised vowels). They are written using the **AGLC**. Mastery of vowels is the basis of reading and writing in Gbáyá.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants
lessons.title: Gbáyá consonants and written production
lessons.anelcac: Consonants — simple, specific, complex; written production of vowels and consonants
objectives: Identify the consonant system of Gbáyá
Recognising specific consonants absent from French
Articulate consonants correctly in context
Writing words with vowels and consonants correctly notated

vocabulary.frenchText: their mothers have been dead for four years
there are five huts in your village
b) he is lying down but he is not sleeping

teacher.intro: Lesson: Gbáyá consonants and written production. Module: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants.
steps: **Setting the context:** Recall the vowels. What is a consonant?
**Presentation:** Table of Gbáyá consonants according to the AGLC. Stress the specific consonants (labio-velars, prenasalised, implosives…).
**Explanation:** Articulating difficult consonants: in isolation → syllable → word.
**Application:** Minimal pairs: listening to words that differ only by one consonant.
**Production:** 5 simple sentences in Gbáyá with careful consonant transcription.
teacher.freedom: Implosive and prenasalised consonants are often the most difficult for students who learned to read and write in French. Repeat the listening activities many times.
teacher.tips: Implosive and prenasalised consonants are often the most difficult for students who learned to read and write in French. Repeat the listening activities many times.

student.intro: After the vowels, here are the consonants of Gbáyá! Some are unique — you will only hear them in Gbáyá and in a few neighbouring African languages.
activities: Listen to the minimal pairs and tick the word you hear (e.g. bìlí / pìlí).
Transcribe 5 dictated words, paying attention to the specific consonants.
Find in the vocabulary all the words containing a prenasalised consonant. How many do you find?
Compose 3 simple sentences in Gbáyá, each with at least one specific consonant.
Memorise: **minimal pair** = two words identical except for one phoneme.
student.memo: The consonant system of **Gbáyá** includes consonants shared with French and specific consonants (implosives, prenasalised, labio-velars…). Writing them according to the **AGLC** is essential for reading and writing.

lessons.title: Definition and functions of tones
lessons.anelcac: Tones — definition, function, presentation; simple tones (high, low, mid)
objectives: Define tone as a distinctive feature of tone languages
Distinguish lexical tone from grammatical tone
Identify the simple tones of Gbáyá
Transcribing words with their tones according to AGLC

vocabulary.frenchText: he throws a fish trap into the river.
the ball of (cassava, maize, millet...etc) is round

teacher.intro: Lesson: Definition and function of tones. Module: Module III — Suprasegmental phonology: tones.
steps: **Setting the context:** Say two Gbáyá words that are written the same but have different tones and different meanings.
**Presentation:** Define tone. Present the simple tones of Gbáyá and their AGLC diacritics.
**Explanation:** Simple tones: high (´), low (`), mid (¯). Have students repeat each tone.
**Application:** Match recorded words with their tone notation.
**Assessment:** Dictation of 5 words — students note the tones.
teacher.freedom: Singing the tones helps to memorise them. Use a flute or whistle the tonal melodies.
teacher.tips: Singing the tones helps to memorise them. Use a flute or whistle the tonal melodies.

student.intro: Gbáyá is a tonal language: the pitch of your voice changes the meaning of the word! You will learn to hear and write down these tones.
activities: Listen to the pairs of words. For each pair, are the tones the same or different?
Transcribe 5 words with their tones using the AGLC diacritics (´ ` ¯).
Find 2 words in the vocabulary that differ only in tone. What does each one mean?
Sing the tones of a 3-syllable word as High-Low-High, then Low-High-Low. What difference do you hear?
Memorise: high tone = ´ ; low tone = ` ; mid tone = ¯.
student.memo: In **Gbáyá**, tone is phonological: it distinguishes words with different meanings. The **simple tones** are high (´), low (`), and sometimes mid (¯). They are written using the **AGLC** diacritics.

lessons.title: Complex tones and tone-marked written production
lessons.anelcac: Complex tones (rising, falling); finding the tone of a word; tonal written production
objectives: Identify the complex tones of Gbáyá (rising, falling)
Finding the tone of a word by the isolation method
Transcribing sentences with full tone marking
Producing a short text in Gbáyá with correct tones

vocabulary.frenchText: he throws a fish trap into the river.
the ball of (cassava, maize, millet...etc) is round

teacher.intro: Lesson: Complex tones and tonal written production. Module: Module III — Suprasegmental phonology: tones.
steps: **Setting the context:** Recall the simple tones. Announce that some syllables carry two tones in succession.
**Presentation:** Complex tones: falling (̂), rising (̌). Let students hear them and reproduce them.
**Explanation:** Isolation method: say the word with an artificial high tone, then a low one, and listen to which sounds natural.
**Application:** Students find the tone of 10 words in Gbáyá using the isolation method.
**Production:** Dialogue of 6 lines in Gbáyá with complete tone notation.
teacher.freedom: The complex falling tone is often the most frequent. Start with it before the rising tone.
teacher.tips: The complex falling tone is often the most frequent. Start with it before the rising tone.

student.intro: You know the simple tones. Now for the complex tones of Gbáyá — syllables that rise and fall at the same time!
activities: Listen to the recorded words and sort them: Simple tone | Complex tone.
Apply the isolation method to 5 words: say them high, then low, and note the tone you perceive.
Transcribe a dialogue of 4 lines in Gbáyá with all the tones marked.
Write a 3-sentence text in Gbáyá about an action from your daily life, with tone marking.
Memorise: falling tone = ̂ ; rising tone = ̌.
student.memo: The **complex tones** of **Gbáyá** (falling ̂, rising ̌) are melodic movements on a single syllable. The **isolation method** makes it possible to find the tone of an unknown word. A transcription in Gbáyá without tones is incomplete.

lessons.title: The noun base and noun classes
lessons.anelcac: NP: constituents, base noun + affixes, noun classes, personal pronouns
objectives: Identify the structure of the noun in Gbáyá (base + affixes)
Recognising the noun classes of Gbáyá
Form the singular and plural of nouns
Use the personal pronouns corresponding to noun classes

vocabulary.langText: àˀ  á  nè  gásá  zú-à  ín zḭá  gé-à
vocabulary.frenchText: he has a big head and a long neck.

vocabulary.langText: à  nón- né  zò-↓áà     wà .... zǒ-wà

teacher.intro: Lesson: The noun base and noun classes. Module: Module IV — The noun phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write a noun in Gbáyá in the singular and plural. What changes?
**Presentation:** Noun class: in Bantu and Bantoid languages, nouns are grouped into classes marked by prefixes.
**Explanation:** Main noun classes of Gbáyá with singular and plural prefixes.
**Application:** Table: singular → plural for 10 nouns.
**Assessment:** Identify the noun class of 5 nouns.
teacher.freedom: Start from the nouns that students already use. Noun classes often correspond to semantic categories (humans, animals, objects…).
teacher.tips: Start from the nouns that students already use. Noun classes often correspond to semantic categories (humans, animals, objects…).

student.intro: In Gbáyá, nouns are organised into **classes**. Each class has its own prefixes for the singular and plural — a much richer system than gender in French!
activities: Using the Gbáyá vocabulary, make a table: Singular | Plural | Noun class.
Identify the class prefix in each noun. Highlight it.
Put the following 5 nouns into the plural by changing the prefix according to the class.
Match each noun with its corresponding class pronoun.
Memorise: **noun class** = grammatical category of nouns, marked by prefixes.
student.memo: In **Gbáyá**, nouns are organised into **noun classes** marked by prefixes. A change of prefix indicates number. Pronouns, adjectives and verbs agree with the class of the noun.

lessons.title: Noun determiners
lessons.anelcac: Determiners: possessives, demonstratives, numerals, indefinites, interrogatives; noun class agreement
objectives: Identify the different types of determiners in Gbáyá
Make determiners agree with the noun according to the noun class
Build complex noun phrases
Producing sentences with complete NPs

vocabulary.langText: àˀ  á  nè  gásá  zú-à  ín zḭá  gé-à
vocabulary.frenchText: he has a big head and a long neck.

vocabulary.langText: à  nón- né  zò-↓áà     wà .... zǒ-wà

teacher.intro: Lesson: Noun determiners. Module: Module IV — The noun phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write a simple noun phrase. How can it be enriched?
**Presentation:** Determiners in Gbáyá: possessives, demonstratives, numerals, indefinites, interrogatives.
**Explanation:** Each determiner agrees with the class of the noun (same class prefix or suffix).
**Application:** Complete noun phrases with the correct determiner according to the class.
**Production:** 5 complex noun phrases (noun + 2 determiners) used in sentences.
teacher.freedom: Stress class agreement — one of the most distinctive features of Gbáyá compared with French.
teacher.tips: Stress class agreement — one of the most distinctive features of Gbáyá compared with French.

student.intro: A noun with its determiners becomes much more precise! In Gbáyá, determiners agree with the **noun class**.
activities: Complete the NPs with the correct possessive determiner according to the noun class.
Underline the determiners in 5 sentences in Gbáyá and identify their type.
Turn each simple noun phrase into a complex noun phrase by adding a demonstrative and a numeral.
Write 5 sentences in Gbáyá with at least two determiners per noun phrase.
Memorise: **class agreement** = the determiner changes form according to the noun class.
student.memo: In **Gbáyá**, all determiners (possessives, demonstratives, numerals, indefinites, interrogatives) agree with the **noun class** of the noun. A **complex NP** = noun + nominal base + agreeing determiners.

lessons.title: The verb stem and conjugation
lessons.anelcac: VP: constituents, stem, affixes, conjugation, verb tenses
objectives: Identify the verb stem and the conjugation affixes in Gbáyá
Conjugate a verb in the main tenses
Analyse the morphological structure of a verb form
Use verb forms correctly in sentences

teacher.intro: Lesson: The verb stem and conjugation. Module: Module V — The verb phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write a verb form in Gbáyá and ask students to identify the stem.
**Presentation:** Break down a verb form: subject prefix + TAM markers + stem + suffixes.
**Explanation:** Conjugation paradigm of a common verb in Gbáyá in several tenses.
**Application:** Conjugation table: 3 common verbs.
**Assessment:** Translate 5 sentences from French into Gbáyá.
teacher.freedom: The TAM system of Gbáyá is often richer than that of French. Start with the most commonly used tenses.
teacher.tips: The TAM system of Gbáyá is often richer than that of French. Start with the most commonly used tenses.

student.intro: The verb is the heart of the sentence in Gbáyá. It alone carries tense, aspect, mood and subject! In this lesson, you take apart the verbal mechanics.
activities: Break down 5 verb forms in Gbáyá: subject prefix | TAM marker | stem | suffix.
Conjugate the verb 'to eat' in Gbáyá in 3 different tenses for all persons.
Identify the tense of 5 sentences in Gbáyá and justify your answer.
Translate 3 sentences from French into Gbáyá, taking care with the conjugation.
Memorise: **TAM** = Tense-Aspect-Mood; this is what verbal affixes express in Gbáyá.
student.memo: In **Gbáyá**, a verb form = subject prefix + TAM markers + stem + suffixes. The **TAM** (Tense-Aspect-Mood) system expresses more precise temporal and aspectual nuances than in French.

lessons.title: Verbal moods and negation
lessons.anelcac: Moods: indicative, imperative; negation; written production of simple/complex VP
objectives: Identify and use the main verbal moods of Gbáyá
Form the verbal negation
Build simple and complex verb phrases
Producing a text with a variety of moods and aspects

vocabulary.frenchText: the man fell from the tree

vocabulary.frenchText: it is birds that fly, not fish

teacher.intro: Lesson: Verbal moods and negation. Module: Module V — The verb phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Give an order in Gbáyá. Which mood is used?
**Presentation:** Moods in Gbáyá: indicative, imperative, and other aspectual moods.
**Explanation:** Formation of the negative in Gbáyá: prefix, negative suffix, or particle.
**Application:** Turn 5 affirmative sentences into negative ones and vice versa.
**Production:** 8-sentence text alternating affirmation, negation and imperative.
teacher.freedom: Negation in Gbáyá can be double (framing the verb) or simple. Show both cases.
teacher.tips: Negation in Gbáyá can be double (framing the verb) or simple. Show both cases.

student.intro: Giving an order, expressing doubt, denying an action — each nuance has its own form in Gbáyá!
activities: Put the 5 given sentences into the negative form.
Turn these 5 statements into imperatives addressed to a friend.
Identify the mood and polarity (affirmative/negative) of each sentence in the text provided.
Write a dialogue of 6 lines including at least 2 imperatives and 2 negations.
Memorise: **mood** = the way of viewing the action; **negation** = grammatical marker denying the action.
student.memo: In **Gbáyá**, the main moods are the **indicative** and the **imperative**. **Negation** is marked by a particle or a specific affix. The diversity of moods is an expressive richness of Gbáyá.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module VI — The sentence in Gbáyá
lessons.title: The simple sentence and its types
lessons.anelcac: Simple, interrogative, negative and imperative sentence; word order
objectives: Analyse the structure of the simple sentence in Gbáyá
Distinguish the 4 types of sentences
Mastering the order of constituents
Producing varied simple sentences

vocabulary.langText: mà-kiì  gásá  tṵ́  tà   àá  sěn  mìi
vocabulary.frenchText: there is a big black stone over there.
there is a tall tree over there
I am taking a small stone.

vocabulary.langText: bé-wáʕ-hḛ̀  n↓é  móyá-à  né  bé-móyá  wáʕ

teacher.intro: Lesson: The simple sentence and its types. Module: Module VI — The sentence in Gbáyá.
steps: **Setting the context:** Read a sentence in Gbáyá. Who does what?
**Presentation:** Basic constituent order in Gbáyá. Compare with French.
**Explanation:** The 4 sentence types from the same basic sentence.
**Application:** Turn declarative sentences into interrogative ones, then into negative ones.
**Production:** 8 varied sentences (2 per type) about school life.
teacher.freedom: Word order in Gbáyá may differ from French. This is a typological feature, not a mistake.
teacher.tips: Word order in Gbáyá may differ from French. This is a typological feature, not a mistake.

student.intro: A well-constructed sentence in Gbáyá follows precise rules. You learn the types of sentences and word order.
activities: Identify the order of constituents in 5 sentences in Gbáyá.
Turn 4 declarative sentences into yes/no questions.
Turn these 4 sentences into negatives.
Write 2 sentences of each type (declarative, interrogative, negative, imperative).
Memorise: the basic order in **Gbáyá** is typologically stable.
student.memo: The **simple sentence** in **Gbáyá** has a characteristic order of constituents. The 4 types (declarative, interrogative, negative, imperative) are formed with specific grammatical markers.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module VI — The sentence in Gbáyá
lessons.title: Logical connectors and the complex sentence
lessons.anelcac: Logical connectors, complex sentence, coordination, subordination; written production
objectives: Identify the logical connectors of Gbáyá
Distinguish coordination from subordination
Build complex sentences
Producing a coherent text with syntactic variety

vocabulary.langText: mà-kiì  gásá  tṵ́  tà   àá  sěn  mìi
vocabulary.frenchText: there is a big black stone over there.
there is a tall tree over there
I am taking a small stone.

vocabulary.langText: bé-wáʕ-hḛ̀  n↓é  móyá-à  né  bé-móyá  wáʕ

teacher.intro: Lesson: Logical connectors and the complex sentence. Module: Module VI — The sentence in Gbáyá.
steps: **Setting the context:** Read a short story in Gbáyá. Which words link the sentences?
**Presentation:** Connectors in Gbáyá: coordinating and subordinating conjunctions.
**Explanation:** Complex sentence by coordination / by subordination. Examples in Gbáyá.
**Application:** Link 5 pairs of simple sentences with the appropriate connector.
**Production:** 10-sentence text on 'A day in my village' with 5 different connectors.
teacher.freedom: The connectors of Gbáyá often have French equivalents but with different syntactic positions.
teacher.tips: The connectors of Gbáyá often have French equivalents but with different syntactic positions.

student.intro: To tell stories and argue, you need to link your sentences. The **logical connectors** of Gbáyá are your tools!
activities: Underline all the connectors in the text provided.
Classify them: Addition | Cause | Consequence | Opposition | Time.
Link 5 pairs of sentences with the most appropriate connector.
Write a text of 8 sentences with at least 4 different connectors.
Memorise: coordination = same level; subordination = one sentence inside another.
student.memo: In **Gbáyá**, **logical connectors** make it possible to build coherent **complex sentences**. Varying syntactic structures improves the quality of written and spoken expression.

lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and interacting in Gbáyá
lessons.anelcac: Everyday communication situations: greetings, introductions, polite expressions
objectives: Mastering greeting formulas according to context
Introducing yourself and someone else in Gbáyá
Use polite and respectful expressions
Holding a short everyday conversation

teacher.intro: Lesson: Greeting, introducing yourself and interacting in Gbáyá. Module: Module VII — Everyday life (Level 1).
steps: **Setting the context:** Two students meet at the market. Act out the scene in French, then ask how to say it in Gbáyá.
**Presentation:** Greetings in Gbáyá according to the time of day, age and context.
**Explanation:** Formulas of respect towards elders, specific to Gbáyá culture.
**Role play:** In groups of 2, simulate encounters in various contexts (market, school, ceremony).
**Production:** Dialogue of 10 lines between two people of different generations.
teacher.freedom: Greeting rules reflect deep cultural values. Value the knowledge of students from families who speak the language.
teacher.tips: Greeting rules reflect deep cultural values. Value the knowledge of students from families who speak the language.

student.intro: Knowing how to greet in Gbáyá means respecting the culture! The greetings change depending on whom you greet and at what time.
activities: Complete the table of Gbáyá greetings: Time | Formula | Expected response.
Play role A: greeting an elder at the morning market.
Make up a dialogue of 8 lines between a child and their grandfather.
Note down 3 Gbáyá politeness formulas with no direct equivalent in French.
Memorise the morning and evening greeting formulas, and those for elders, in Gbáyá.
student.memo: **Greetings** in **Gbáyá** vary according to the time of day, status and social context. They reflect the community's values of respect and solidarity.

lessons.title: Express everyday needs and actions
lessons.anelcac: Real-life situations: shopping, requests for help, travelling, daily activities
objectives: Express everyday needs in Gbáyá
Describe daily activities
Use vocabulary for places and actions of everyday life
Producing a descriptive text on a typical day

teacher.intro: Lesson: Expressing everyday needs and actions. Module: Module VII — Everyday life (Level 1).
steps: **Setting the context:** Images of scenes from daily life — market, field, school, home. How can they be described in Gbáyá?
**Presentation:** Thematic vocabulary: food, travel, household activities.
**Simulation:** Market scene: buyer and seller in Gbáyá.
**Application:** Describe your day in Gbáyá (from waking up to going to bed).
**Production:** 10-sentence text: 'My day in Gbáyá'.
teacher.freedom: Everyday vocabulary is the most motivating. Link the ALCAM words to real situations.
teacher.tips: Everyday vocabulary is the most motivating. Link the ALCAM words to real situations.

student.intro: You know how to greet people. Now you are going to manage in everyday situations in Gbáyá: at the market, on the road, at home.
activities: Match each picture of a scene from daily life with the corresponding word or sentence in Gbáyá.
Play the role of the seller at the market: answer the requests in Gbáyá.
Write 5 sentences describing your morning activities from the time you wake up.
Translate these 5 sentences about daily journeys into Gbáyá.
Memorise 10 everyday words in Gbáyá with their French translation.
student.memo: The **everyday** vocabulary in **Gbáyá** covers food, getting around and household activities. Mastering it allows functional communication in all contexts.

lessons.title: Argue and persuade in Gbáyá
lessons.anelcac: Elaborate communication: argumentation, narration, formal speech
objectives: Build a simple argument in Gbáyá
Use the expressions of formal speech
Narrating a past event coherently
Delivering a 2-minute oral speech in Gbáyá

teacher.intro: Lesson: Arguing and persuading in Gbáyá. Module: Module VIII — Everyday life (Level 2).
steps: **Setting the context:** Read a proverb in Gbáyá. Ask students to explain it and defend it.
**Presentation:** Formulas of formal oral speech in Gbáyá: forms of address, opening, closing.
**Explanation:** Structure of an argument: thesis → arguments → examples → conclusion.
**Practice:** Debate: for or against the use of Gbáyá at school? Each group defends its position.
**Production:** 2-minute speech on a given theme.
teacher.freedom: Public speaking is highly valued in Cameroonian cultures. Draw on this tradition to motivate the students.
teacher.tips: Public speaking is highly valued in Cameroonian cultures. Draw on this tradition to motivate the students.

student.intro: In Gbáyá cultures, well-spoken words are a force. You learn to argue and persuade with eloquence.
activities: Identify in the text: thesis, arguments, examples.
Prepare 3 arguments to defend the teaching of Gbáyá in primary school.
Give an opening speech for a ceremony in Gbáyá.
Narration: tell in Gbáyá about a memorable event from your school life.
Memorise the opening and closing formulas of a formal speech in Gbáyá.
student.memo: **Argumentation** in **Gbáyá** follows this pattern: thesis → arguments → examples → conclusion. **Formal speech** follows precise cultural conventions. Mastery of elaborate oral expression is a high-level skill.

lessons.title: Oral literature and advanced written production
lessons.anelcac: Oral literature: proverbs, tales, riddles; long written production
objectives: Analyse the structure of a tale or a riddle in Gbáyá
Identify the themes and values conveyed
Writing a short tale following the conventions of the genre
Using oral literature as a teaching resource

teacher.intro: Lesson: Oral literature and advanced written production. Module: Module VIII — Everyday life (Level 2).
steps: **Setting the context:** Tell or play a short tale in Gbáyá.
**Presentation:** Genres of oral literature: tales, proverbs, riddles, epics.
**Analysis:** Structure of the tale: initial situation → disruption → events → resolution → moral.
**Application:** Analyse a tale provided, following this structure.
**Production:** Tale of at least 15 lines in Gbáyá with an explicit moral.
teacher.freedom: Oral literature is a threatened cultural treasure. Invite community storytellers if possible.
teacher.tips: Oral literature is a threatened cultural treasure. Invite community storytellers if possible.

student.intro: Gbáyá tales, proverbs and riddles are literary works in their own right. You will analyse them and you will create your own!
activities: Read the tale provided and identify the 5 stages of its narrative structure.
Identify 3 moral values taught by this tale.
Translate a proverb in Gbáyá into French and explain its figurative meaning.
Write a short tale (15 lines) in Gbáyá with a moral about work or respect.
Memorise: tale = fictional narrative with an educational purpose; proverb = brief formula of collective wisdom.
student.memo: The **oral literature** of **Gbáyá** (tales, proverbs, riddles) transmits the values of the community. The tale has a 5-stage structure. Writing it in Gbáyá draws on all the language skills acquired.

lessons.title: Who are the Gbaya? Identity, language and territory
lessons.anelcac: Cultural areas, cultural identity, settlement
objectives: Name the Gbaya community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Gbaya community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Gbaya community to them: who are they, where do they live, where did they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Gbaya community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Gbaya community: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Gbaya call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Majority group in its village, living on good terms with its neighbours; many also speak Ewondo. • Gbaya is spoken in several regions (Adamawa, North, East, Centre, South) and, beyond, in Central African Republic, Sudan and Nigeria. • People used to marry among the Gbaya; today, they marry whom they like. • Ancestral land, with purely Gbaya neighbourhoods; other groups have been added. • Tradition has the Gbaya coming from Egypt, through Sudan and Central African Republic.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: A people with a warrior tradition and of hunters, present in several regions of Cameroon and as far as the Central African Republic, Sudan and Nigeria, the Gbaya live here alongside the Makaa of the North, the Bobilis, the Kpere, the Kako and the Bamvələ. Initiation into the labi once structured social life; today largely Christianised, they remain attached to traditional remedies and maize beer.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Gbaya community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover the Gbaya community: its name, its language, its neighbours and its history.

activities.title: I understand the name
activities.instruction: Explain the name the Gbaya (Gbaya) give themselves and its meaning.

activities.title: I locate
activities.instruction: On a map, place the community, its region and its neighbours.

activities.title: I trace the history
activities.instruction: On a timeline or a map, draw the migration route told in tradition.

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare the origin of this people with that of your own community: 2 similarities, 2 differences.

student.memo: A people with a warrior tradition and of hunters, present in several regions of Cameroon and as far as the Central African Republic, Sudan and Nigeria, the Gbaya live here alongside the Makaa of the North, the Bobilis, the Kpere, the Kako and the Bamvələ. Initiation into the labi once structured social life; today largely Christianised, they remain attached to traditional remedies and maize beer.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Gbaya
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
objectives: Identify traditional authorities
Explain how decisions are made
Identifying the rules of deference
lessons.competence: Describe how the Gbaya organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision has to be made for the whole Gbaya village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Gbaya organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “An important decision has to be made for the whole village of the Gbaya. Who decides, and how?” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Patriarchal society: decisions are taken within the family and the father has the final say. • One inherits within one's own clan; daughters' children do not inherit. • Men's and women's societies handed down from generation to generation: the initiates and those in charge of widowhood rites. • Children greet first; the wife does not look her husband in the eyes, as this would be contempt.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Patriarchal society: decisions are taken within the family and the father has the final say. People inherit within their own clan; daughters' children do not inherit. Men's and women's societies passed down from generation to generation: the initiates and those in charge of widowhood rites.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Gbaya, then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: How do the Gbaya live together? Who decides, and how do people show respect to one another?

activities.title: I draw a diagram
activities.instruction: Draw the organisation chart: chief, notables, families, population.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Describe the path of a decision, from discussion to public announcement.

activities.title: I pick out
activities.instruction: Note down two rules of respect or deference and explain their meaning.

activities.title: I debate
activities.instruction: In groups: what are the advantages of making decisions by consensus?

student.memo: Patriarchal society: decisions are taken within the family and the father has the final say. People inherit within their own clan; daughters' children do not inherit. Men's and women's societies passed down from generation to generation: the initiates and those in charge of widowhood rites.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Gbaya
lessons.anelcac: Ways of life: culinary practices
objectives: Naming traditional foods and drinks
Describe a preparation
Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Gbaya, describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Gbaya.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Gbaya, describe how they are prepared and draw out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Gbaya.” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: cassava couscous, salt-and-chilli sauce (tɔ́ŋ nɛ ndónge). • Drinks: ndolo / kpata (maize beer). • Men: hunting, clearing land, livestock rearing. Women: tilling, sowing, harvesting, trade.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Gbaya eat mainly cassava couscous, tɔ́ŋ nɛ ndónge. Traditional drinks: maize beer. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Gbaya: write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Find out what the Gbaya traditionally eat and drink.

activities.instruction: Ask an elder how one of these dishes is prepared and write down the steps.

activities.title: I match
activities.instruction: Link each dish to the group's activities (agriculture, fishing, livestock rearing…).

activities.title: I present
activities.instruction: Prepare a poster for the class food fair.

student.memo: The Gbaya eat mainly cassava couscous, tɔ́ŋ nɛ ndónge. Traditional drinks: maize beer. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Clothing, adornments and crafts of the Gbaya
lessons.anelcac: Ways of life: clothing practices, crafts
objectives: Describe traditional clothing
Identify craft objects and their use
Explain the criteria of beauty
lessons.competence: Describe the clothing, adornments and craft objects of the Gbaya, and explain their use and value.
lessons.situation: A museum asks you to prepare a display on the clothing and crafts of the Gbaya.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, craft objects or photos of craft objects, recycled materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the clothing, adornments and craft objects of the Gbaya, and explain their use and value.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “A museum asks you to prepare a display case on the clothing and crafts of the Gbaya.” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How did people dress in the past, and how do they dress today? — Do clothes indicate status or occasion? — What objects are made, from what materials, and for what uses? — What are the criteria of beauty?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Old clothing of woven bark (ndumbu) and leaves (yakɛdɛ), then saro, gandoura and wrappers. • Crafts were formerly organised in castes, which have since disappeared. • Beauty: scars, filed teeth, musculature and a fine voice for men; tattoos and filed teeth for women.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Old clothing of woven bark (ndumbu) and leaves (yakɛdɛ), then saro, gandoura and wrapper cloths. Crafts were once organised in castes, which have since disappeared. Beauty: facial scars, filed teeth, muscular build and a fine voice for men; tattoos and filed teeth for women.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw and label a garment or craft object of the Gbaya, stating its material, use and occasion.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Gbaya
lessons.anelcac: Key events: birth, naming, initiation
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth
Describe how names are given
Describe the passage to adulthood
lessons.competence: Explain how the Gbaya welcome a child, give them a name and mark their entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born into a Gbaya family. How will he or she be named, and how will he or she become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Gbaya welcome a child, give them a name and mark their entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “A child has just been born into a Gbaya family. How will the child be named, and how will they become an adult?” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Twins' names: Ngozo and Yabub for boys, Toza and Zeri for girls. • The names of the deceased are given again so that they do not disappear; the name does not change. • Certain names are not spoken, on pain of a fine; one says dâ (the father) and na (the mother). • A child who is born is welcomed as a warrior, a fighter. • A boy becomes a man through initiation into the labi; for a girl, her behaviour and maturity are observed.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Names of twins: Ngozo and Yabub for boys, Toza and Zeri for girls. The names of the dead are given again so that they do not disappear; the name does not change. Certain names are not pronounced, on pain of a fine; people say dâ (the father) and na (the mother).

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Explain the meaning of three Gbaya personal names and describe the moment when a child receives their name.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Marriage and bride price among the Gbaya
lessons.anelcac: Key events: marriage
objectives: Putting the stages of marriage in order
Explain the symbolism of the bride price
Comparing yesterday and today
lessons.competence: Describe the stages of traditional Gbaya marriage, the bride price items and their symbolism.
lessons.situation: Your elder brother wants to marry a young Gbaya woman. Which steps will he have to follow?
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, props for the staging.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the stages of the traditional Gbaya marriage, the elements of the bride price and their symbolism.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “Your older brother wants to marry a young Gbaya woman. Which steps will he have to follow?” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who chooses the spouse? Do people marry within the group or outside it? — What are the stages of marriage? — What does the bride price include, and what does each item symbolise? — Where does the couple live after the marriage?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Patrilineal kinship; the wife settles with her husband. • The boy becomes a man through initiation into the labi; for a girl, her behaviour and maturity are observed. • In the past, a girl was sometimes promised from birth to seal a friendship. • It is the young man's aunts who make the first move; it also happened that a young girl went of her own accord to live with her suitor. • No bride price in money: the conduct of the son-in-law is observed. The symbolic gifts are a chicken, a spear, a mat and a knife, emblems of a warrior people; offering others would bring bad luck to the couple's children.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: No bride price in money: the conduct of the son-in-law is observed. The symbolic gifts are a chicken, a spear, a mat and a knife, emblems of a warrior people; offering others would bring misfortune on the couple's children.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: In a group, role-play the marriage request among the Gbaya, then explain the meaning of two items of the bride price.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.memo: No bride price in money: the conduct of the son-in-law is observed. The symbolic gifts are a chicken, a spear, a mat and a knife, emblems of a warrior people; offering others would bring misfortune on the couple's children.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Leisure: traditional music and dances of the Gbaya
lessons.anelcac: Community practices: leisure, traditional dances
objectives: Identify dances and their occasions
Describe a dance and its instruments
Perform the dance
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Gbaya, choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and act it out.
lessons.situation: Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class prepares a Gbaya dance performance for the cultural day.
lessons.materiel: Instruments or recordings, costumes, clear space.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Gbaya, choose the most representative one, describe it, draw out its cultural significance and act it out.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “Participation in cultural life in the family and in society: the class is preparing a Gbaya dance performance for the cultural day.” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Which dances are practised, and on what occasions? — Who dances (men, women, children, initiates)? When and where? — Which instruments, songs and outfits are used? — What is the cultural meaning of the chosen dance?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Rhythms: labi (vigorous, linked to initiation), patenge, yɔŋgɔ, kɛkɛ, awunda, on the drum (bīo). • The yaorop is danced at deaths; the tabi at the end of initiation or at the death of an initiate. • The festivals of the harvests, the return of the rains and the start of the dry season are no longer held.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Among the Gbaya, the traditional dances (death dances, tabi) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: drum. Festival(s): mɔinam.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Describe a dance of the Gbaya (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

student.memo: Among the Gbaya, the traditional dances (death dances, tabi) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: drum. Festival(s): mɔinam.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Gbaya
lessons.anelcac: Community practices: traditional economy
objectives: Identify economic activities
Explain the division of tasks
Explain access to land
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Gbaya, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Gbaya. First you need to understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Gbaya, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “A development project wants to help the Gbaya. First, we need to understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Men: hunting, clearing, livestock. Women: ploughing, sowing, harvesting, trade. • Land belongs to everyone; each person farms the plots inherited from their parents. • Crafts were formerly organised in castes, now disappeared.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: hunting, land clearing, livestock rearing. Women: ploughing, sowing, harvesting, trade. Land belongs to everyone; each person farms the plots inherited from their parents.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Make a two-column table (men / women) of the activities of the Gbaya, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Gbaya
lessons.anelcac: Community practices: symbolism, rites, taboos
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
Identify sacred places
Explain the role of taboos
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Gbaya, and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Gbaya. Which places and rules must they absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Gbaya, and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “A visitor arrives among the Gbaya. What places and rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following elements: • Certain families perform an ancestral rite when a woman is pregnant, even far from the village. • The child who is born is welcomed as a warrior, a fighter. • Death mobilises the whole community, which seeks out its causes (ndoŋ awù). • Most of the old sacred places have disappeared; yet a mystical rock announces deaths. • Taboo of incest. Prohibitions: the child gives their first game to their father; men eat neither panther (kɔ́yɔ́) nor wild boar entrails, which they hand over to their parents in exchange for their blessing.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Some families perform an ancestral rite when a woman is pregnant, even far from the village. The child who is born is welcomed as a warrior, a fighter.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Gbaya (3 places or rules to respect, with the reason for each).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.memo: Some families perform an ancestral rite when a woman is pregnant, even far from the village. The child who is born is welcomed as a warrior, a fighter.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Gbaya
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day
Introducing yourself
Counting from 1 to 10

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Gbaya and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Gbaya family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in sharing the kola nuts while counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Gbaya and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “You are visiting a Gbaya family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the kola nuts by counting.” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The language of the community is Gbaya. • Greeting formulas: Mosamɛ = Hello (neutral formula, at any time); Mɛ nɛ = morning greeting (one person); Mosa enɛ = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Pɔ̍k, Yίto, Tar, Nar, Mɔrɔ. • The founding ancestor, Mbartoua, is “the one who blocks the door”. • The absence of bride price in some families and mistrust of the hospital set the Gbaya apart, though in other respects they resemble the groups of the Centre and the South.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Gbaya are the first steps towards communicating with the Gbaya. Polite expressions show the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Gbaya.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Gbaya are the first steps towards communicating with the Gbaya. Polite expressions show the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
